analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare for seniors and disabled beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill won 121 cosponsors in the House but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare today does not cover most dental care, eyeglasses, routine eye exams, or hearing aids, so tens of millions of older and disabled Americans pay for these out of pocket or buy separate private policies. This bill would add all three to Medicare: cleanings, fillings, dentures, annual eye exams and eyewear, and hearing exams and hearing aids, with phased-in federal payment levels and limits on how often items can be replaced. It was introduced in the House and referred to two committees, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 65 million people on Medicare would gain coverage for dental care, eyeglasses and contact lenses, and hearing aids — services they currently pay for themselves or forgo. Low-income beneficiaries would get full federal payment faster under the bill's special rule for subsidy-eligible individuals.

how_it_helps.text: Adds dental and oral health services to Medicare, including preventive care, basic and major services, emergency dental care, and dentures [S2] [S3].
Adds routine eye exams, eyeglasses, contact lenses, and low vision devices to Medicare, with federal payment covering 80 percent of allowed charges [S2] [S3].
Adds routine hearing exams, audiology services, and hearing aids, repealing the current statutory exclusion of hearing aids from Medicare coverage [S3].

Gives low-income, subsidy-eligible beneficiaries full federal payment for dental services from 2025 onward, faster than the general phase-in, which starts at 30 percent in 2025 and reaches 80 percent in 2027 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers, since the bill creates a new Medicare entitlement with no dedicated financing source; beneficiaries would still owe the standard 20 percent coinsurance on covered services.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no dedicated funding source for the new benefit, so it would increase federal Medicare spending by the full cost of coverage, which independent cost estimates of similar proposals have put at tens of billions of dollars per year.

Coverage is partial and phased in: non-preventive dental services start at only 30 percent federal payment in 2025 and reach 80 percent in 2027, eyeglass lenses are capped at $100 per year, and dentures and hearing aids are limited to one set every five and four years respectively [S3].
The Secretary of Health and Human Services could impose prior authorization and other limits on all three benefits, which could delay or restrict access in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large for a group that often skips dental and hearing care because of cost, and the bill's phased-in payment levels, frequency limits, and Secretary discretion are an attempt to control cost. The main honest objection is that it adds a major open-ended entitlement with no revenue to pay for it, and the first years of dental coverage would be thin. Weighing that against the current status quo, where older Americans pay full price out of pocket or go without, the design is reasonably careful but the financing question is unanswered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced and referred again to a health subcommittee; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2023 by Rep. Lloyd Doggett with 77 original cosponsors and attracted 121 Democratic cosponsors in total [S3] [S4].
The Speaker referred it to both the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day of introduction, and it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health on January 9, 2023 [S5].
Nearly two years later, on December 17, 2024, it was again referred to the Subcommittee on Health — the only other action in its entire history [S5].
No markup, hearing vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill never advanced out of committee before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries are no better off — they continue to pay out of pocket for dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids. Standalone dental and vision insurance companies and Medicare Advantage plans, which market dental, vision, and hearing coverage as reasons to choose their private policies, kept their market position untouched.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 77 original cosponsors on day one.

for.name: 121 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, roughly a quarter of the House Democratic caucus
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of adding dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare; every cosponsor was a Democrat [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire two-year Congress without a markup or committee vote; it was referred to a health subcommittee twice and never advanced [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled the floor agenda in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, as is standard for a bill with no committee action and no support from the majority.

sides.party_line_note: All 121 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no Republican is on record supporting it; the bill sat in committees of a Republican-controlled House for its entire life.

industries.industry: Standalone dental and vision insurance companies
industries.note: Millions of seniors buy separate dental and vision policies or pay out of pocket; a comprehensive Medicare benefit would displace much of that market. The bill's failure preserves their revenue from older customers.

Dental, vision, and hearing extras are a key marketing advantage of private Medicare Advantage plans over traditional Medicare; adding these benefits to traditional Medicare would erode that edge. The bill would also change how these services are paid inside Medicare. Its death leaves the Advantage plans' selling point intact.

industries.industry: Dentists, optometrists, and hearing aid providers
industries.note: The bill would create a large new pool of paying Medicare patients for dental, eye, and hearing care. Had it passed, their patient volume would have grown alongside seniors' access.
